In proof of the unerringly beneficial effects of such good beginnings upon all large classes of human beings, we have only to point to many of those manufactories in Am America, which are of recent foundation, and in which the right track was at once struck into. The condition of the operatives, male and female, at the Lowell factories, in Massachusetts, has frequently been spoken of by travellers with surprise. Mr Dickens, in his late tour, visited the place, and, like others, was astonished at the progress which had been made in intellectual cultivation, good manners, refined taste, and economic habits. Speaking of the factory girls, he says-" They are all well dressed; and that phrase necessarily includes extreme cleanliness. They had serviceable bonnets, good warm cloaks, and shawls; and were not above clogs and pattens. Moreover, there were places in the mill in which they could deposit these things without injury, and there were conveniences for washing. They were healthy in appearance, many of them remarkably so, and had the manners and deportment of young women, not of degraded brutes of burden. We have been informed, that, in another manufacturing town, Cupar, the proportion is about the same as in Dundee. In Glasgow, few factory girls wear shoes or stockings, but nearly all contrive to decorate themselves with ear-rings, a circumstance indicating a low standard of taste and general comfort.

In further alluding to the Lowell factory females, Mr Dickens mentions a fact noticed by us on a former occasion. These young women have got up among themselves a periodical called the Lowell Offering, a repository of original articles of no mean literary merit. Many of the boarding-houses, he says, keep a piano for the use of the inmates, and nearly all the young ladies subscribe to circulating libraries. In these facts, we have shadowed out to us what both male and female operatives, in many parts of England, might become, under more careful management. Accustomed to contemplate the working-classes in a degrading position, many will fail to comprehend how they should be capable of improving their station in society. But there is really nothing in existing arrangements to prevent such a result. The problem is to be wrought out by the united efforts of benevolence, and the exertions of the working-classes themselves. Mechanics' Institutions, extended in the sphere of their operation, and improved by the infusion of recreative entertainments, may do something; national education, on a broad and liberal basis, would do more; and the operatives, once stirred up to exert themselves as individuals in the great object of practical melioration, the day might be said to be gained; the victory won.
